messages.author: 0e0df690b737d734
messages.subject: multiple repetitions
parts:
Hi there,

as most people do, let me first thank you for this excellent package
you are putting together.

I have a question about ezANOVA. Most of my data comes from
experiments where each subject in each condition performs multiple
repetitions of a task. This is the classic approach where the
measurements are averaged, then analyzed with a single averaged
measurement in each condition.

With ezANOVA, I was thrilled to find how easy it is to skip the
averaging step and directly analyze the raw data, indicating in wid
the identity of each subject. The software seems to be clever enough
to make sense of what's going on by taking account of which trials
were performed by the same person in the same condition and which in a
different condition.

What I would like to know is what ezANOVA is actually doing here. As
far as I can tell, it is not averaging the multiple trials, because
the result is different. In fact, the outcome if the ANOVA from
ezANOVA is more conservative, which tells me that it's probably taking
the variance of the many trials in a condition into account?

Yesterday I spent time trying to replicate the same outcome in Minitab
(where, admittedly, I'm a newbie) and I didn't manage to get it right.

Could you please shed a bit of light on this question and explain what
ezANOVA does in this type of analysis?

Much appreciated!

messages.author: cb25d91fd630a4e5
messages.subject: Re: [ez4r] multiple repetitions
parts:
Actually, ezANOVA does indeed collapse each cell of the design to an
average within each level of wid before computing the ANOVA.

To what software are you comparing when you observe that ezANOVA
appears to be more conservative?

If you want a tool that *does* take into account the amount and
variance of the raw data, check out ezMixed (though I'd suggest you
use the dev version: http://www.github.com/mike-lawrence/ez).

parts:
Dear Mike,

Thank you for the wonderful and helpful package.
And for this helpful email list.
Following you conversation with DJP I would like to add a related question/request.

I notice, from time to time, that you recommend the usage of ezMixed over ezAnova.
I read the description of the function and it turns out to be "above my statistical head".

Can you recommend on a manuscript that explains the cases where ezMixed is more appropriate, hopefully free and in rather introductory-medium level of statistical knowledge?

Thanks again
dror

messages.author: cb25d91fd630a4e5
messages.subject: Re: [ez4r] multiple repetitions
parts:
Here's the history:

ez was originally developed to automate procedures that I was doing
repeatedly in my own work (collapse conditions to a mean, do an anova,
produce follow-up plots, etc). I subsequently learned about mixed
effects modelling and have thus completely eliminated anova from my
own work as mixed effects modelling is demonstrably superior with
regards to:

- fewer assumptions (no sphericity assumption, simply normality of residuals)

- robustness to missing data

- accounting for raw data features (amount & variance)

- easy to incorporate generalized additive modelling, which
elegantly/powerfully permits non-linear effects of continuous
predictor variables

- easily computable evidence metrics (computing likelihood ratios for
ANOVA can be a pain)

- proper treatment of binomial data as such (see the Dixon and Jaeger
refs I cite frequently on this list)

- elegant signal-detection-theory-based analysis of binomial data
(Sheu & Shih, 2008)

- easy to compute error bars that do not include between-Ss variance
(which is usually not of inferential interest)

As a consequence of seeking to automate my own use of mixed effects
models, I developed the ezMixed function for ez. I hope to write
manuscript descriptions of ezMixed (likely to be submitted to JASA &
BRM) in the very near future that will provide a low-complexity
description of its approach (with citations to more in-depth papers
from which my approach has been inspired). Until then, I'm afraid
you're stuck with the following mid/high-complexity sources from which
ezMixed draws its inspiration:

General texts on Mixed effects models:
- Pinheiro, J. C., & Bates, D. M. (2000). Mixed Effects Models in S
and S-Plus (p. 528). Springer. Retrieved from
http://www.amazon.com/Mixed-Effects-Models-S-S-Plus/dp/0387989579
- Baayen, R. H. (2008) Analyzing Linguistic Data. A Practical
Introduction to Statistics Using R. Cambridge University Press. (See
chapter 12; pdf:
http://www.ualberta.ca/~baayen/publications/baayenCUPstats.pdf)
- Bates (in progress: http://lme4.r-forge.r-project.org/book/)

Power of mixed effects models for linguistic research
- Baayen, R. H., Davidson, D. J., & Bates, D. M. (2008). Mixed-effects
modeling with crossed random effects for subjects and items. Journal
of Memory and Language, 59(4), 390-412. Elsevier Inc.
doi:10.1016/j.jml.2007.12.005

Proper analysis of binomial data:
- Dixon, P. (2008). Models of accuracy in repeated-measures designs.
Journal of Memory and Language, 59(4), 447-456. Elsevier Inc.
doi:10.1016/j.jml.2007.11.004
- Jaeger, T. F. (2008). Categorical Data Analysis: Away from ANOVAs
(transformation or not) and towards Logit Mixed Models. Journal of
memory and language, 59(4), 434-446. Elsevier Inc.
doi:10.1016/j.jml.2007.11.007

SDT-based analysis of binomial data:
- Sheu, C.-F., Lee, Y.-S., & Shih, P.-Y. (2008). Analyzing recognition
performance with sparse data. Behavior Research Methods, 40(3),
722-727. doi:10.3758/BRM.40.3.722

Generalized additive modelling as a means to elegantly/powerfully
account for linear and potential non-linear effects of a continuous
predictor:
- Wood, S. N. (2006). Generalized Additive Models: An Introduction
with R. Chapman and Hall/CRC.

Likelihood ratios as properly scientific metrics of evidence:
- Glover, S., & Dixon, P. (2004). Likelihood ratios: a simple and
flexible statistic for empirical psychologists. Psychonomic bulletin &
review, 11(5), 791-806. Retrieved from
http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15732688
- Johansson, T. (2011). Hail the impossible: p-values, evidence, and
likelihood. Scandinavian journal of psychology, 52(2), 113-25.
doi:10.1111/j.1467-9450.2010.00852.x

AIC as asymptotically equivalent to leave-one-level-out
cross-validation for mixed effects models:
- Fang, Y. (2011). Asymptotic equivalence between cross-validations
and Akaike Information Criteria in Mixed-Effects Models. Journal of
Data Science, 9, 15-21.

You could also check out the posts tagged with "mixed-model" at
stat.stackexchange.com, for example:

http://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/13166/rs-lmer-cheat-sheet

http://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/17233/how-to-explain-linear-mixed-models-to-laypeople

http://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/4700/what-is-the-difference-between-fixed-effect-random-effect-and-mixed-effect-mode

http://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/764/linear-mixed-effects-models

http://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/5414/pitfalls-of-linear-mixed-models

Hi Mike,

many thanks for your answer. It's good to know that all ezANOVA does
is exactly what I normally do manually. What happened yesterday was
that I made some mistake in the manual calculation of averages, and I
concluded that ezANOVA was probably doing something more
sophisticated. I've done the same exercise of comparison and, indeed,
the result is spot on. Apologies for the confusion.

Sometime soon I hope to be looking into ezMixed, so thank you for
pointing me to it.
